title: The Mode, Ties and Non-Numeric Data
unit: Mean, Median, Mode and Standard Deviation
quickIdea: The mode is the value with the highest frequency; a data set can have no mode, one mode, or several, and the mode is the only one of the three summaries that also works for categories.
remember: Mode = the value of maximum frequency. Count frequencies first; nothing else is needed.
If every value occurs once there is no mode. Some texts instead say every value is a mode; state which convention you are using rather than assuming one.
Two values tied at the top give a bimodal data set; more than two give a multimodal one. A tie is a property of the data, not a mistake in the calculation.
The mode ignores how far the other values are from it. Moving a non-modal value from 100 to 10000 changes the mode not at all.
The mode is the only measure of centre that makes sense for nominal data - a colour, a brand, a city - because a mean or a median needs order or arithmetic.
For a continuous variable the mode is the point where the density peaks, and for a grouped table it is the modal class refined by an interpolation formula.
In a unimodal, moderately skewed distribution the three summaries are ordered, and the mode sits at the far end from the tail.

example.work: Frequencies: 2 once, 3 twice, 5 once, 7 three times, 9 once. The largest frequency is 3, at the value 7. For comparison, the mean is 43/8 = 5.375 and the median, the average of the fourth and fifth values 5 and 7, is 6.
example.answer: The mode is 7, the only mode.

gateAngle: No GATE CSE engineering-mathematics question asks for a mode on its own. The mode appears in 2011 Q.33 as the statistic whose index position survives the transformation y = ax + b, and in the aptitude papers as part of a mean-median-mode relation.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Give the mode or modes of 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, and then of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
variations.answer: The first list is bimodal with modes 2 and 3; the second has no mode under the strict convention.
variations.why: In the first list two values tie at frequency 2, so neither is more typical than the other. In the second every frequency is 1, so no value is more frequent than any other.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A grouped table has classes 10-20, 20-30, 30-40, 40-50 with frequencies 5, 9, 14, 8. Which class is the modal class, and what is the mode?
variations.answer: The modal class is 30-40 and the mode is 34.55.
variations.why: L = 30, f1 = 14, f0 = 9, f2 = 8 and h = 10, so mode = 30 + ((14-9)/(2*14 - 9 - 8))*10 = 30 + (5/11)*10 = 34.545. The modal class is the answer the table alone can justify; the interpolation is the refinement, and it is an approximation because the values inside a class are assumed evenly spread.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: X has a Poisson distribution with mean lambda = 2.4. What is its mode?
variations.why: The ratio P(X=k)/P(X=k-1) = lambda/k exceeds 1 exactly while k < lambda, so the mass increases up to floor(lambda) and decreases after it. With lambda = 2.4 the largest mass is at 2, not at the rounded 2.4.

trap.what: Reporting the mean when the mode was asked for, or insisting on a single mode when two values tie.
trap.why: The three summaries answer three different questions, and a tie is a legitimate outcome. A single number cannot always be reported for the mode.
trap.counterexample: For 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 the mean is 2.5 and both 2 and 3 are modes; writing 'the mode is 2' discards half of the answer, and writing 'the mode is 2.5' answers a different question.

check.question: Find the mode of 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 9.
check.explanation: The frequencies are 4: 2, 5: 1, 6: 2, 7: 3, 9: 1. The largest is 3 at the value 7, so 7 is the unique mode and the data is unimodal.
